title: How Many Copies: Counting What a Vector Does, and the One Word That Keeps It From Copying

questions.question: A program stores a few thousand objects and is slower than the arithmetic says it should be. Nothing leaks. Where might the cost be?
options: Copies that are not on any line of the source: in parameters, in a vector growing and in returns
questions.explanation: A type that counts its own copies and moves makes them visible.

questions.question: What does a vector do when it grows, and the move constructor is not marked noexcept?
options: Copies every element, since a move that might throw half way cannot be undone

questions.question: What does reserve(n) change about filling a vector with push_back of temporaries?
options: It removes the moves of growth, leaving one move per temporary, 100 for 100 packets
questions.explanation: The growth part depends on the library, so a test checks that it goes and not its size.

questions.question: What does emplace_back(i) do differently from push_back(Packet(i))?
options: It builds the object where it will live, so there is no temporary to move: 0 copies and 0 moves
questions.explanation: It passes the arguments on to the constructor.

questions.question: A vector of 50 is passed to a function by value from a variable. How many copies?
options: 50: a parameter by value is a new vector and every element is copied
questions.explanation: By const reference it was 0, and from std::move 0 copies and 0 element moves.

questions.question: A test finds 0 copies and 0 moves for a returned vector. What should a careful reader remember?
options: The compiler can remove copies and moves altogether, so zero may be its work and not the code's
questions.explanation: Counts show what happened, not what the code guarantees.
